commentary.text: I’m claiming a central square immediately with Red, establishing an anchor for a potential four-square center occupation while keeping the piece supported by flexible edge pieces.
I claim a central square immediately and place Blue beside the advanced Red piece, creating a future sandwich target while supporting a center-occupation push with Green.
Yellow takes the opposite central square, building a diagonal Team A foothold. Red also retains the tactical option of landing at (3,5) to sandwich Blue’s center piece against the Red piece at (3,3).
I’m claiming a second central square, creating a strong Blue–Green foothold while restricting the nearby Yellow piece’s horizontal movement.
Red executes the prepared sandwich: landing at (3,5) traps the Blue piece at (3,4) against Red’s central anchor. This scores Blue’s first loss and clears a central square for Team A.
I’m blocking Yellow’s immediate route to (4,2), which would sandwich and capture our Green piece on (4,3). The Blue piece also gains a useful interior position for a later central advance.
The earlier route was blocked by Blue at (6,2). Yellow instead moves beside that piece, creating a sandwich threat: a later Yellow landing at (6,3) could trap Blue against this new flank.
I’m using the advanced Green piece on (4,3) as the far flank: landing on (2,3) sandwiches and captures the Red piece on the central square (3,3), disrupting Team A’s center control.

Red reoccupies (3,3), safely stepping between the two Green pieces because moving into a sandwich does not trigger capture. This restores the central anchor and prevents Green from simply claiming that square.
I’m pulling the exposed Blue piece out of Yellow’s immediate sandwich threat while keeping it near the center for future support.

Yellow advances to (4,1), preparing to land at (4,2) and sandwich Green’s central piece against Yellow at (4,4). Green must now abandon or reposition that blocker, while the same pattern discourages Blue from replacing it.
I’m shifting Green beside the center, keeping the existing central foothold while preparing to occupy (3,4) or pressure Yellow’s central piece.

Red shifts to (3,4), placing itself beneath Green at (2,4). This prepares a vertical sandwich: Red’s edge piece at (0,4) can later land at (1,4) and capture that Green piece. The move also preserves tactical control of the central row.
I’m blocking Yellow’s immediate move from (4,1) to (4,2), which would sandwich and capture our Green center piece at (4,3). This also develops Blue beside the center.

Yellow develops to (5,3), keeping the four-piece horizontal tension intact while cutting off Green’s downward escape from (4,3). Green must either remain tied to Blue’s blocker or retreat upward and surrender the lower central square.
I’m using the Green piece on (4,3) as the fixed flank, capturing Yellow on (5,3) while advancing another Green piece toward the center.
Red completes the prepared vertical sandwich, landing at (1,4) to trap Green at (2,4) against Red at (3,4). This answers Yellow’s loss with Green’s first loss.
I’m occupying the gap between Red’s vertical pair, safely disrupting its capture structure while creating a threat to sandwich the Red–Yellow center column from below.

Yellow vacates (4,1) to open a direct Red tactic along row 4. If Green leaves the central chain intact, Red can descend from (0,1) to (4,1) and sandwich both Blue at (4,2) and Green at (4,3) against Red at (4,4)’s vertical file counterpart—specifically the Red piece at (3,4) is not on that row. Wait: that means no Red far flank exists at (4,4), since (4,4) is Yellow. This tactic is invalid.

Instead, Yellow keeps the endpoint and develops toward Green’s lower piece, taking (6,2) as one side of a future horizontal trap.

I’m exploiting the Green flank on row 4: landing at (4,0) sandwiches the Yellow and Blue pieces against Green at (4,3). The friendly-fire cost is significant, but it puts Yellow one capture from elimination and clears a congested line near the center.

Red steps off (1,4) while preserving the lower Red flank at (3,4). This creates an immediate return threat: moving back to (1,4) would sandwich Blue at (2,4) for its third loss, so Blue must spend its turn escaping or obstructing the landing square.
I’m exploiting the Blue anchor on (2,4): landing on (5,4) sandwiches the Yellow and Red pieces above it, eliminating Yellow and clearing two central squares for a center-occupation push.

With Yellow eliminated, this Void move cannot capture, so its best value is positional. The Void Yellow advances to (3,5), one step from the central square (3,4), where it can contribute to Team A’s center occupation and obstruct Blue and Green.
I’m opening the central file while occupying (3,3), setting up a coordinated center-occupation threat with Blue advancing to (3,4) and the rear Green piece later filling (4,3).

Red advances to (4,2), approaching the vacant lower central square while avoiding any immediate sandwich. With Green occupying (3,3), Team A needs a second route into the center rather than relying solely on the Void Yellow at (3,5).
I’m occupying a second central square with Blue, setting up Green to take (4,3) and threaten completion of all four center squares.
Void Yellow moves to (4,5), positioning directly beside the last open central square. It cannot capture, but it can occupy (4,4) on a later Yellow turn if Team A can keep that square available.
I occupy the third central square, setting up Blue to complete the four-square center on its next turn. Red cannot reach the remaining center square immediately.
Red reinforces the lower-left approach with a second piece, keeping the pieces connected and avoiding an immediate capture while contesting space beside Green’s central column.
I complete the four-square center with Blue, securing immediate center-occupation victory for Team B.
